title: Optimizing Cognitive Architecture
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos uses Carl Hendrick's anecdote about a colour-matching phonics puzzle as a lens for seven lessons about instructional design in reading. The puzzle let his daughter succeed through perceptual cues rather than blending sounds, which Janetos extends to common classroom practices: sorting words by sight, predictable texts, word coffins, three-cueing and oral-only phonemic awareness work. Her central claim is that tasks must require the thinking they are meant to develop, otherwise students gain an illusion of competence and surface-level victories that leave long-term memory untouched. She draws on Kirschner, Willingham, Bjork, Shanahan and Seidenberg, and adds her own experience with intervention students who search pictures instead of decoding. She also criticises engagement as a proxy for learning and emphasises opportunity costs. The article is a clear bridge between the science of reading and the science of learning.
points: A task that can be completed through surface cues, like colour matching or reading pictures, produces success without the intended skill and leaves cognitive architecture unchanged.
Predictable text and instructional-level reading give students the illusion of competence and block orthographic mapping through decoding.
Engagement, such as visible turn-and-talk, is a poor proxy for learning and can reward shallow processing.
Oral-only phonemic awareness work is inefficient compared with integrating letters, and every unproductive activity carries an opportunity cost.
quotes: Although I’ve been steeped in the Science of Reading (SOR) over the last two decades thanks to the books by cognitive psychologist Diane McGuinness, the Science of Learning is a relatively new field for me. However, it turns out that effective reading methods are effective because they adhere to learning principles that are an integral part of SOR approaches to reading instruction, so there is a synergy between the two fields that can support and guide teachers. Learning about learning facilitates teaching reading.

Depending on the nature of the text, a student’s instructional level is oftentimes below grade-level, which means a student is reading material with simpler vocabulary and syntax. This situation can impede comprehension in subsequent years due to lack of exposure to and familiarity with academic vocabulary and sophisticated sentence structure inherent in complex text. Reading these instructional-level texts can give students the illusion of competence, which may provide initial reassurance but is ultimately counterproductive.

I remember only one thing from the only economics class I’ve taken, and that is the law of alternative costs, how, for example, one bomb might cost three hospitals. More commonly in education, we refer to opportunity costs: time spent assembling phonics puzzles that don’t require reading is time lost engaging in activities that do.

It goes without saying that we have no time to waste on lessons that do not develop deep learning. Unlike a horse to water, we do have ways to lead our students to whatever we are teaching them AND make them learn it—as long as making involves adhering to the principles of cognitive science. Our students come already equipped with cognitive architecture; our job is to show them how to make themselves at home in their heads in order to make learning happen.
